channel.title: Chen-Yang Su — Blog
channel.description: Notes on evaluating AI systems, building agents for science, and human genetics.

item.title: The uncomfortable truth about power: why merit alone is not enough
item.description: In 1847 a Vienna doctor named Ignaz Semmelweis made medical students wash their hands, and deaths among new mothers in his clinic fell by almost 90%. Two years later he was out of a job. Stanford professor Jeffrey Pfeffer argues that doing good work and getting people to adopt it are two different skills, and that the second one can be learned.

item.title: The seven deadly sins of product design, and what they miss
item.description: Reid Hoffman says social networks do best when they tap into one of the seven deadly sins. The sins explain why someone signs up. They explain much less about what happens to that person afterward.

item.title: When the answer is cheap
item.description: Xiaoyin Qu predicts that AI will drive the value of every task with a checkable answer to zero, leaving profit only in matters of taste. When answers get cheap, the premium moves to choosing the questions and checking the answers.

item.title: When AI agents bypass the middleman
item.description: An AI agent might find the same rental for less on a host's site. The hard part is proving that the offer is real and the booking is safe. That is where Airbnb's fee faces its test.

item.title: When the buyer has an agent
item.description: Patrick Collison expects personal AI agents to act as a structural subsidy for product quality. Agents will raise the reward for quality only where quality can be verified independently of the seller.

item.title: How to get luckier
item.description: Some people get lucky more often than others. Most of the difference comes down to noticing more and knowing people outside your usual circle.

item.title: Rejection is data
item.description: Of the NeurIPS papers one committee accepted, a second committee rejected 50.6%. One rejection is a noisy observation.

item.title: How to know when to change course
item.description: Persistence pays only when it is aimed at the right thing. Commit to the problem, and treat each solution as a hypothesis you are ready to drop.

item.title: What are the important problems in your field?
item.description: Most people choose a role and inherit its problems. Choose the problem first, then find the role that lets you work on it.

item.title: The paradox of ambition
item.description: Lottery winners were barely happier than people living nearby. Ambition runs into the same problem. Each achievement quietly becomes the new baseline.

item.title: Choosing the game
item.description: A high salary and a high-leverage career are not the same thing. The difference is how closely your earnings are tied to your own time.

item.title: Optimism in the face of uncertainty
item.description: My MSc advisor Joëlle Pineau took the title of her commencement address from bandit algorithms. An action is worth taking not because its estimated reward is high, but because the uncertainty around it leaves room for it to be much better.

item.title: The problem with calling models open or closed
item.description: Anthropic is the notable exception among the major labs, and critics see protectionism from a company whose business depends on keeping its own models closed. Both interpretations can be true.
